public_rationale: The literal claim that every company invested in AI fails: the Atlanta Fed's March 25, 2026 report says nearly 60% of responding firms invested in AI during 2025 [e1]. The majority-returns clause is supported qualitatively: BCG's September 30, 2025 report says 60% reported minimal revenue and cost gains despite substantial investment, while a minority achieved larger benefits [e2].
limitations: The surveys do not establish worldwide company prevalence.
BCG's self-reported results may concern particular business areas rather than whole companies and do not establish standardized, audited net returns on investment.
BCG's September 2025 publication does not establish results for the full calendar year.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: Although every company is investing in AI, most are so far not getting huge returns from it.

statement.excerpt: Every company is investing in AI, but so far most aren’t getting huge returns.

from_speaker: Every company is investing in AI
our_interpretation: Assess the universal investment statement separately from the majority-returns statement.
Every is read literally, while acknowledging that it may be conversational exaggeration. Most means more than half.
Investing includes actual spending on AI tools, services or development, rather than merely considering or using AI.
Huge returns means substantial realized financial benefits relative to investment costs. No numerical threshold is invented.
Use 2025, the latest completed calendar year that could be broadly reported before the post, for the ongoing observation.
These are cross-business prevalence claims, not amounts in a named company's accounts; metric_scope is null.
criteria.support_condition: Evidence establishes universal AI investment and shows that more than half of companies have not realized substantial financial returns. Support for only the majority clause is identified separately.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Evidence of companies making no AI investment contradicts the universal clause. Evidence that most companies have realized substantial returns contradicts the majority clause. Opposite findings for the two clauses warrant mixed.

evidence.locator: Eighty percent of firms will invest in AI during 2026, and large firms invest the most, first paragraph
evidence.explanation: Actual investment was far from universal among surveyed firms, including large firms. This directly contradicts the literal every-company clause without relying on adoption as a spending proxy.

A majority reporting minimal financial gains despite substantial investment supports the ordinary reading of the majority-returns clause. The same article describes a successful minority, so this does not imply that large returns were absent everywhere.
